newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Jospin plans change on jobs, immigration.
newsitem.headline: France's Jospin plans change on jobs, immigration.

text.p: France's opposition Socialist party said on Friday it would change economic policy to promote jobs without raising public spending and that it would repeal the country's most controversial laws on immigration if elected.

The Socialists said in their manifesto for a parliamentary election at the end of the month that they supported a European single currency but that the economic fitness criteria should be interpreted flexibly, that all European Union countries should be involved and that there should be a European economic government.

The manifesto, released ahead of a news conference later on Friday, proposed a reform of payroll charges to cut the cost of labour, a government-backed scheme to create 700,000 jobs and a cut in the work week to 35 hours from 39 without loss of salary.
The Socialists also proposed cutting Value Added Tax (VAT) on basic goods, easing housing tax on lower income families and raising wealth tax.
Education would become the top budget priority in a country where the ruling centre-right coalition was cutting the number of teachers, the manifesto says.
On immigration, the Socialists said they would repeal the controversial "Pasqua" and "Debre" laws which tightened the controls on immigration under the current coalition.
"We will develop new ways of fighting illegal immigration and vigourously penalise companies which fail to respect the law," the manifesto text says.
"We will introduce a cooperation policy with the countries concerned in order to control immigration flows."

The Socialists, trailing the centre-right in opinion polls on the likely victors of the two-round election on May 25 and June 1, vowed to protect public services in security, education, transport, health, post and telecoms.
"We reject privatisation of public services and turning them into groups devoted to profit," the manifesto says.

It said its goal of creating 700,000 jobs for the young -- including 350,000 public sector jobs -- would be funded by scrapping other ineffective job creation schemes and that the plan would not mean raising public spending.
French unemployment is at a record 12.8 percent of the workforce despite a slight fall recently in the total number out of work.
